Home.metadataTitle: Jainism: the soul, karma, and liberation
Home.metadataDescription: Learn how Jain traditions understand the soul, karma, ahimsa, and liberation. Explore Jain teachings, prayers, texts, and history.
Home.title: Jainism: the soul, karma, and liberation
Home.lead: Jain traditions teach that each living being has a soul and that karmic matter binds the soul to rebirth. The path to moksha (liberation) calls for right faith, knowledge, conduct, and ahimsa.
Home.guideNote: Explore each topic on its own. This is a reading map, not a sequence of spiritual steps.

steps.title: Jīva · soul
steps.description: Every living being has a soul, distinct and capable of liberation.

steps.title: Karma
steps.description: Karma binds the soul and shapes its experience of rebirth.

steps.title: Ahimsa
steps.description: Nonviolence guides conduct toward living beings.

steps.title: Moksha
steps.description: Liberation is release from karma and rebirth.

Start.metadataTitle: Six reading paths through Jain thought
Start.metadataDescription: Follow reading paths on Jain ideas about the soul, karma, ahimsa, liberation, cosmology, history, and texts.
Start.title: Six paths through Jain thought
Start.lead: Begin with the soul and karma, then follow the ideas that connect ethics, liberation, cosmology, stories, and Jain texts.

paths.title: Jainism: core ideas
paths.description: An introduction to jīva, karma, ahimsa, Mahavira, and the communities that carry Jain teachings forward.
questions: How are knowledge, conduct, and liberation connected?

paths.title: Soul, karma, and moksha
paths.description: Jain philosophy describes the soul as conscious and karma as subtle matter that binds to it. Moksha is release from karma and rebirth.
questions: Why is karma called subtle matter in Jain philosophy?
How does moksha differ from a favorable rebirth?

paths.title: Jain cosmology and time
paths.description: Explore loka, aloka, and the repeating cycles of time in Jain cosmology.
questions: What do Jain texts mean by loka and aloka?
What do the six eras in a time cycle describe?

paths.title: Ahimsa and the vows
paths.description: Ahimsa shapes Jain vows. Anekāntavāda asks how a subject can be understood from different standpoints.
questions: How do mendicant vows differ from lay vows?
How does anekāntavāda make room for more than one standpoint?

paths.title: Jain stories and history
paths.description: Meet figures such as Ṛṣabha, Bāhubali, Mahavira, and Malli through Jain narratives and historical study.
questions: What do Jain narratives and historical sources tell us about these figures?
How do Śvetāmbara and Digambara accounts of Malli differ?

paths.title: Jain texts and communities
paths.description: Learn about Jain scriptures, commentaries, languages, teachers, and the fourfold community.
questions: How do Śvetāmbara and Digambara textual traditions differ?
Who makes up the fourfold Jain community?

Practice.title: Prayer, reflection, and observance
Practice.description: Jain devotional life includes recitation, worship, repentance, study, and annual observances. Explore the Navkar Mantra, pratikraman, Paryushan, Dashalakshana, and more.

entries.title: Navkar Mantra
entries.description: A Jain prayer honoring the five supreme beings: the arihants, siddhas, acharyas, upadhyayas, and sadhus.

entries.title: Chattari Mangalam
entries.description: A Prakrit verse naming four auspicious refuges: the arihants, siddhas, sadhus, and dharma.

entries.title: Logassa Sutra
entries.description: A Prakrit hymn praising the twenty-four Tirthankaras.

entries.title: Bhaktamar Stotra
entries.description: A Sanskrit hymn in praise of Ṛṣabhanātha, the first Tirthankara.

entries.title: Uvasaggaharam Stotra
entries.description: A Prakrit hymn in praise of Pārśvanātha.

entries.title: Khamemi Savva Jive
entries.description: A verse of forgiveness and goodwill toward all living beings.

entries.title: Pratikraman
entries.description: A practice of reviewing one’s conduct, expressing repentance, and asking forgiveness.

entries.title: Paryushana and Das Lakshana
entries.description: Paryushan among Śvetāmbaras and Dashalakshana among Digambaras: annual periods of study, restraint, and reflection.

Privacy.title: Privacy
Privacy.intro: This page explains what the library stores when you use a Google account to save your reading and notes.
Privacy.signin: Google provides this site with a stable account ID, your verified email address, and your display name. The site does not receive your Google password and does not ask for access to other Google services.
Privacy.reading: When you are signed in, the library stores topics you open, mark complete, or save for later. This information is used to show your reading history and saved list in your account.
Privacy.notes: Notes are saved with the topic you wrote them about. They are private to your account and are not shown to other readers or librarians. Notes are stored as plain text.
Privacy.storage: Account details, reading activity, saved topics, and notes are stored in the library's Cloudflare D1 database. A secure, HttpOnly cookie keeps your browser signed in for up to 30 days. The database stores a hash of the session token.
Privacy.manage: You can sign out from your account page to revoke the current browser session. You can also delete your account there; this removes the account record, active sessions, reading history, saved topics, and notes from the live database.
Privacy.staff: Librarians can use the separate library review workspace. Reader notes and reading activity are not included in that workspace.
Privacy.google: Google handles the sign-in step under its own privacy policy. The library only requests the basic OpenID Connect profile and email information needed to create and secure your account.
